media.transcript: This thing tracks mosquitoes the way an air defense system tracks aircraft, then shoots them down with a laser. It is called Photon Matrix from a startup in Changzhou in eastern China. A lidar sweeps a flat fan of light across the room, constantly measuring how far away the background is. When something small crosses that plane, the distance reading changes. If the size matches a mosquito, the system fires. The company says it reads a target's distance, orientation and body size in about 3 milliseconds and can handle 30 mosquitoes a second. The laser goes down the same optical path the lidar used, aimed at the wings. Range is a 6 meter radius across a 90 degree scan for insects 2 to 20 millimeters, flying slower than 1 meter per second. There is a visible blue laser version for outdoors and an invisible infrared one for bedrooms. For safety, it needs a solid background inside its range. If it cannot find one, the laser shuts off. The Chinese model costs around 638 dollars, but they're not shipping them yet and not even in production.

candidates.caption:
Nobody switched from CPUs to GPUs because GPUs are "faster."

They're not, really. One GPU core is worse than one CPU core at almost
everything. Slower. Dumber. Can barely make a decision.

There are just 16,384 of them.

That's the thing that clicks when you look at how AI chips actually evolved.
Every jump was a trade. Give something up, get something back.

The CPU gives up nothing. 8 cores that run your OS, open a tab and handle a
mouse click, all at once. Total flexibility. It just works through a problem a
few values at a time, which is fine for everything except the one thing neural
networks do: the same operation across millions of values at once.

So the GPU gave up smart. Thousands of tiny cores that only do simple math, but
do it simultaneously. Graphics needed exactly that, millions of pixels, one
calculation. Turns out a matrix multiply is the same shape of work. Accident of
history. AI ran on gaming hardware for a decade.

Then people noticed the real bottleneck was never the math.

A 32-bit multiply costs about 3.7 picojoules. Fetching the numbers to multiply
it with, out of DRAM, costs 640.

173x more expensive to MOVE data than to USE it.

Every AI chip since is a response to that one fact.

Google's TPU gave up generality. Its systolic array is a grid of tiny
calculators wired to each other, so data walks in once and gets handed cell to
cell, reused the whole way across instead of re-fetched. An 8x8 multiply goes
from 1,536 memory trips to 192. And the 8x isn't a tuning result. It's just how
wide the grid is.

Your phone gave up precision. It had to. A data centre accelerator pulls 700
watts. Point that at an iPhone battery and it's flat in 65 seconds. So NPUs
round the numbers off, INT8 instead of FP32, 0.2 pJ instead of 3.7, and the
model barely notices. That's face unlock. Background blur. Live speech. None of
it touching the cloud.

Four chips, one idea turned up each time: work out what you're willing to lose.

Which trade surprised you?

#aihardware #gpu #npu #tpu #cpu

media.transcript: GPUs, TPUs, MPUs, these are some of the most important chips powering AI right now, but what actually makes them different? To understand that, you need to understand one thing first. Modern AI is basically doing an enormous amount of matrix multiplication, again and again and again. Neural networks take huge grids of numbers, multiply them together, add the results, and repeat that process billions of times. The difference between all these chips is mostly about how specialized they are for doing that math. Let's start with the CPU. The CPU is the general purpose chip inside almost every computer. It has a relatively small number of very powerful cores designed to do almost anything. Run your operating system, open a webpage, execute some code, respond to your mouse click. A CPU can absolutely run AI models. The problem is that neural networks need the same kind of calculation performed across millions of values at the same time, and CPUs simply weren't designed for that level of parallelism. That's where GPUs came in. GPUs were originally built for graphics. To render a game, your computer needs to perform similar calculations across millions of pixels simultaneously. So instead of a few extremely powerful cores, GPUs have thousands of smaller cores working in parallel. And it turns out that architecture is incredibly good for neural networks too. That's why GPUs became the dominant hardware for training and running large AI models. But GPUs are still fairly general purpose. So what if you build a chip specifically for AI? That's basically the idea behind Google's TPU. TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. Instead of being designed for graphics first, TPUs are optimized specifically for the tensor and matrix operations used heavily in machine learning. One important design is something called a systolic array. Imagine a huge grid of tiny calculators. Data enters the grid, moves from one calculator to another, and gets reused along the way. Instead of constantly going back to memory for every operation, the data keeps flowing through the chip. That reduces memory movement, which is extremely important because moving data can sometimes cost more time and energy than doing the actual multiplication. Now what about NPUs? NPU stands for Neural Processing Unit. These are also specialized AI accelerators, but you'll often find them inside phones, laptops, and other edge devices. Here the problem is different. You don't have a giant data center with thousands of watts of... You have a battery. So the goal becomes run AI locally while using as little power as possible. MPUs are optimized for efficient neural network operations, often using lower precision math that AI models can handle perfectly well. That's why your phone can do things like face recognition, background removal, camera enhancement, speech processing, which are even run smaller generative AI models without sending everything to the cloud or destroying your battery. So the easiest way to remember this is CPU, general purpose computing, GPU, massive parallel computing, TPU, highly specialized machine learning acceleration, NPU, efficient AI acceleration, especially on edge devices. And there are even more acronyms appearing now, LPUs, VPUs, but almost all of them are chasing the same goal. Take the math AI uses the most and build hardware that can do that specific math faster, cheaper, or with less power.

plan.tagline: From cluttered photo to clear product image.
plan.promise: Remove the background, choose a solid color, adjust brightness, and export a clearer listing image while preserving the physical product and its details.
plan.question: Which visual demonstration makes the editing steps clearest while showing that the product’s details stay unchanged?
